Reduction to a single closed equation for 2 by 2 reaction-diffusion systems of Lotka-Volterra type.

Martin Strugarek ††thanks: AgroParisTech, Paris, France; Sorbonne Universités, UPMC Univ Paris 06, CNRS, INRIA, UMR 7598, Laboratoire Jacques-Louis Lions, Équipe MAMBA, 4, place Jussieu 75005, Paris, France.    Nicolas Vauchelet ††thanks: Sorbonne Universités, UPMC Univ Paris 06, CNRS, INRIA, UMR 7598, Laboratoire Jacques-Louis Lions, Équipe MAMBA, 4, place Jussieu 75005, Paris, France.
August 24, 2026
Abstract

We consider general models of coupled reaction-diffusion systems for interacting variants of the same species. When the total population becomes large with intensive competition, we prove that the frequencies (i.e. proportions) of the variants can be approached by the solution of a simpler reaction-diffusion system, through a singular limit method and a relative compactness argument. As an example of application, we retrieve the classical bistable equation for Wolbachia’s spread into an arthropod population from a system modeling interaction between infected and uninfected individuals.

Keywords: Reaction-diffusion systems; model reduction; asymptotic analysis: population dynamics.

2010 AMS subject classification: 35K57, 92D25.

1 Introduction

We are interested in modeling situations when two biological populations of the same species interact with each other, especially move, reproduce and compete. The dynamics of these two populations are commonly described by a reaction-diffusion system of two equations in the whole space ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} (d≥1d\geq 1). In this setting, reaction terms encompass the whole interaction. Usually, they are non-linear, in order to account for competition or mutualistic interaction. Denoting n1​(t,x)n_{1}(t,x) and n2​(t,x)n_{2}(t,x) the densities of each species’ variant at time t>0t>0 and position x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, the mathematical model reads:

{∂tn1−∇⋅(A(x)∇n1)=n1​f1​(n1,n2),∂tn2−∇⋅(A(x)∇n2)=n2​f2​(n1,n2),\begin{cases}\partial_{t}n_{1}-\nabla\cdot(A(x)\nabla n_{1})&=n_{1}f_{1}(n_{1},n_{2}),\\ \partial_{t}n_{2}-\nabla\cdot(A(x)\nabla n_{2})&=n_{2}f_{2}(n_{1},n_{2}),\end{cases} (1)

where the diffusion matrix AA is elliptic and the regular functions f1f_{1} and f2f_{2} describe the interaction between variants. This system is complemented with initial conditions. Since the analysis of such systems is actually delicate, one prefers considering the proportion of one population, for instance p=n1n1+n2p=\frac{n_{1}}{n_{1}+n_{2}}. Then the interactions are described through the dynamics of the proportion pp by a reaction-diffusion system:

∂tp−∇⋅(A(x)∇p)=pF(p).\partial_{t}p-\nabla\cdot(A(x)\nabla p)=pF(p). (2)

Since the pioneering works of Fisher [7] and Kolmogorov, Petrovskii, Piskunov [15], this kind of reaction-diffusion equation has been extensively studied in mathematical literature. In particular many effort have been done to establish the existence of traveling waves and to describe the invasion phenomena (see e.g. [6], [21]). However, when considering systems of reaction-diffusion equations, many difficulties make such analysis harder. For instance, we mention the work [9] for competitive system. The aim of this paper, is to focus on the link between system (1) and (2). More precisely, the main question we want to address is to know if solutions of system (1) can be rigorously approximated by system (2) for the proportion pp of one species. In our main result, we show that under suitable assumptions on the reaction terms in (1), the proportion p=n1n1+n2p=\frac{n_{1}}{n_{1}+n_{2}} is close (in a sense which will be defined below) to a solution to system (2). More precisely, we show that when the total population becomes large with intensive competition, the frequency p=n1n1+n2p=\frac{n_{1}}{n_{1}+n_{2}} for system (1) converges to the solution of equation (2) where the non-linear function in the right hand side FF is explicitely given with f1f_{1} and f2f_{2}. Our proof is based on a compactness argument resulting from a priori estimates. The closest results of model reduction for competition-diffusion systems, are those of [10] and [11] (in bounded domains, with a specific and extensive discussion on the boundary issues).

Our first interest in this topic comes from the biological phenomenon of cytoplasmic incompatibility, caused by the endo-symbiotic bacterium Wolbachia in some arthropod species (see [23], [2], [13]). These bacteria have gained interest lately because of their potential use as a tool to fight arboviruses (see [12], [22]). For this situation, modeled by a reaction-diffusion system, we prove that if reaction terms scale in a proper way, then the frequency of Wolbachia infection approaches the solution of a single closed reaction-diffusion equation, which is bistable. Bistable equations have been suggested long ago for this problem (see [2] for an account on this topic, and [19] for a specific discussion). When these models encompass a space-dependent total population density ρ\rho (as proposed e.g. in [17, 1, 2]), they read

∂tp−∇⋅(A(x)∇p)−2∇ρρA(x)∇p=pF(p).\partial_{t}p-\nabla\cdot(A(x)\nabla p)-2\frac{\nabla\rho}{\rho}A(x)\nabla p=pF(p). (3)

In some sense our result justifies their use thanks to a rigorous singular limit method. We do not assume that ρ\rho and pp vary independently, and find that (3) must be corrected since FF is a function of pp and ρ\rho. We warn the reader that in order to simplify the computations, we will define a “reduced total population density” nn, instead of using the total population density ρ\rho directly.

The outline of the paper is the following. In the next Section, we present the setting of the problem. In particular the assumptions on the reaction terms and the main result are presented. Section 3 is devoted to an example of application: the interaction between an infected and an uninfected mosquitoes population. A numerical illustration is also provided in dimension d=1d=1. The proof of our main result is provided in Section 4. This proof relies strongly on a priori estimates that make us able to prove relative compactness of solutions families when a parameter describing the size of the population goes to +∞+\infty. We give in Section 5 some extension to our main result. Finally, Section 6 highlights questions this work opens.

2 Setting of the problem for typical Lotka-Volterra systems

In this section, we first define the setting where our result applies (typical Lotka-Volterra systems), and then state it in Theorem 1.

2.1 System and assumptions

For ϵ>0\epsilon>0, let f1ϵ,f2ϵ:ℝ2→ℝf_{1}^{\epsilon},f_{2}^{\epsilon}:\mathbb{R}^{2}\to\mathbb{R} be two functions. We start from the following system in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}

{∂tn1ϵ−∇⋅(A(x)∇n1ϵ)=n1ϵ​f1ϵ​(n1ϵ,n2ϵ),∂tn2ϵ−∇⋅(A(x)∇n2ϵ)=n2ϵ​f2ϵ​(n1ϵ,n2ϵ),\begin{cases}\partial_{t}n_{1}^{\epsilon}-\nabla\cdot(A(x)\nabla n_{1}^{\epsilon})&=n_{1}^{\epsilon}f_{1}^{\epsilon}(n_{1}^{\epsilon},n_{2}^{\epsilon}),\\ \partial_{t}n_{2}^{\epsilon}-\nabla\cdot(A(x)\nabla n_{2}^{\epsilon})&=n_{2}^{\epsilon}f_{2}^{\epsilon}(n_{1}^{\epsilon},n_{2}^{\epsilon}),\end{cases} (4)

with given initial data niϵ​(t=0,x)=niinit,ϵ≥0n_{i}^{\epsilon}(t=0,x)=n_{i}^{\text{init},\epsilon}\geq 0 for i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\}. We assume that the matrix AA is elliptic and that f1ϵ,f2ϵf_{1}^{\epsilon},f_{2}^{\epsilon} are smooth enough to guarantee existence and uniqueness of a global solution for fixed ϵ>0\epsilon>0. More precisely,

Assumption 1 (Ellipticity and symmetry of AA).

The diffusion matrix A:ℝd→ℝd×dA:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} is symmetric and the system (4) is uniformly elliptic, i.e.

∃ν0∈ℝ+∗,∀x,ζ∈ℝd,ζ⋅(A⁡(x)​ζ)≥ν0​|ζ|2,\exists\nu_{0}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{*},\forall x,\zeta\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\,\zeta\cdot(A(x)\zeta)\geq\nu_{0}\lvert\zeta\rvert^{2},

where |⋅|\lvert\cdot\rvert stands for the euclidean norm in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}.

We define “reduced total population” nϵn^{\epsilon} and frequency (i.e. proportion of population 11) pϵp^{\epsilon} by

nϵ:=1ϵ−n1ϵ−n2ϵ,pϵ:=n1ϵn1ϵ+n2ϵ.n^{\epsilon}:=\frac{1}{\epsilon}-n_{1}^{\epsilon}-n_{2}^{\epsilon},\quad p^{\epsilon}:=\frac{n_{1}^{\epsilon}}{n_{1}^{\epsilon}+n_{2}^{\epsilon}}. (5)

Since 00 is a sub-solution for each equation in (4), and since initial data are nonnegative, we have niϵ​(t,⋅)≥0n_{i}^{\epsilon}(t,\cdot)\geq 0, for any t≥0t\geq 0. By convention, we take pϵ=0p^{\epsilon}=0 whenever n1ϵ=n2ϵ=0n^{\epsilon}_{1}=n^{\epsilon}_{2}=0.

We want to compute the limit as ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0 of the frequency pϵp^{\epsilon} under the above assumption on A:ℝd→ℝd×dA:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} and on some assumptions on the families of functions (f1ϵ,f2ϵ)ϵ>0(f_{1}^{\epsilon},f_{2}^{\epsilon})_{\epsilon>0}.

As a typical Lotka-Volterra system, we note that absence of either population of type 11 or 22 is a solution to this system: there is no spontaneous generation of one population from the other. In addition, the system is positive: for non-negative initial data, 0≤pϵ≤10\leq p^{\epsilon}\leq 1. Now, we state our key assumptions.

Assumption 2 (Dependence in ϵ\epsilon).

Functions f1ϵ,f2ϵf_{1}^{\epsilon},f_{2}^{\epsilon} are of class 𝒞2​(ℝ+2−{0})\mathcal{C}^{2}(\mathbb{R}_{+}^{2}-\{0\}), and for i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\} there exists Fi∈𝒞2​(ℝ+2)F_{i}\in\mathcal{C}^{2}(\mathbb{R}_{+}^{2}) (independent of ϵ>0\epsilon>0) such that

fiϵ​(n1ϵ,n2ϵ)=Fi​(nϵ,pϵ).f_{i}^{\epsilon}(n_{1}^{\epsilon},n_{2}^{\epsilon})=F_{i}(n^{\epsilon},p^{\epsilon}). (6)

In other words, for any n1,n2≥0n_{1},n_{2}\geq 0, we may write fiϵ​(n1,n2)=Fi​(1ϵ−n1−n2,n1n1+n2)f_{i}^{\epsilon}(n_{1},n_{2})=F_{i}(\frac{1}{\epsilon}-n_{1}-n_{2},\frac{n_{1}}{n_{1}+n_{2}}).

Adding the two equations in system (4) and using also the identity

2.2 Main result

We are now in position to state our main result. We recall that we associate to any initial data niinit,ϵn_{i}^{\text{init},\epsilon} the corresponding solutions of (4), (niϵ)(n_{i}^{\epsilon}), and their relative variable nϵn^{\epsilon} and pϵp^{\epsilon}, as defined in (5). In addition we may define

ninit,ϵ=1ϵ−n1init,ϵ−n2init,ϵ,pinit,ϵ=n1init,ϵn1init,ϵ+n2init,ϵ.n^{\text{init},\epsilon}=\frac{1}{\epsilon}-n_{1}^{\text{init},\epsilon}-n_{2}^{\text{init},\epsilon},\quad p^{\text{init},\epsilon}=\frac{n_{1}^{\text{init},\epsilon}}{n_{1}^{\text{init},\epsilon}+n_{2}^{\text{init},\epsilon}}.
Theorem 1.

We assume that Assumptions 1, 6, and 3 are satisfied. We consider the solutions of (4) with initial data niϵ​(t=0)=niinit,ϵ∈L∞​(ℝd,ℝ+)n_{i}^{\epsilon}(t=0)=n_{i}^{\text{init},\epsilon}\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{R}_{+}) for i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\}. We assume moreover that there exists pinit∈L2​(ℝd)p^{\text{init}}\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) such that

pinit,ϵ​⇀ϵ→0​pinit​ in ​L2​(ℝd)−weak,ninit,ϵ−h⁡(0)∈L2∩L∞​(ℝd),p^{\text{init},\epsilon}\underset{\epsilon\to 0}{\rightharpoonup}p^{\text{init}}\mbox{ in }L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})-\mbox{weak},\quad n^{\text{init},\epsilon}-h(0)\in L^{2}\cap L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), (11)

with uniform bounds in ϵ>0\epsilon>0.

{pϵ→ϵ→0p0​ strongly in ℋT1, weakly in ​ℋT2,nϵ−h⁡(pϵ)→ϵ→00​ strongly in ℋT1, weakly in ​ℋT2,\begin{cases}p^{\epsilon}\xrightarrow[\epsilon\to 0]{}p^{0}\text{ strongly in $\mathcal{H}^{1}_{T}$,}\text{ weakly in }\mathcal{H}^{2}_{T},\\ n^{\epsilon}-h(p^{\epsilon})\xrightarrow[\epsilon\to 0]{}0\text{ strongly in $\mathcal{H}_{T}^{1}$,}\text{ weakly in }\mathcal{H}^{2}_{T},\end{cases} (12)

where p0p^{0} is the unique solution of the following initial value problem

{∂tp0−∇⋅(A(x)∇p0)=p0F1(h(p0),p0),p0​(t=0)=pinit.\begin{cases}\partial_{t}p^{0}-\nabla\cdot(A(x)\nabla p^{0})=p^{0}F_{1}(h(p^{0}),p^{0}),\\ p^{0}(t=0)=p^{\text{init}}.\end{cases} (13)

This result asserts that, locally in time, the proportion of the first population, pp, solution to system (4), under suitable assumption on the reaction term and on the initial data, is close to the solution of a single reaction-diffusion system (13). This latter system have been intensively studied, in particular existence of traveling waves, describing propagation phenomena (see e.g. [6], [21]). The main interest in this reduction process is that since the behavior of solutions to the scalar equation (13) is well-known. Therefore we can deduce, for small values of ϵ\epsilon, the local in time behavior of solutions to (4).

We observe that the limit reaction term r⁡(p):=p​F1​(h⁡(p),p)r(p):=pF_{1}(h(p),p) in (13) satisfies

r⁡(0)=0,r⁡(1)=F1​(h⁡(1),1)=0,r(0)=0,\qquad r(1)=F_{1}(h(1),1)=0,

because H⁡(h⁡(p),p)=0=−p​F1​(h⁡(p),p)−(1−p)​F2​(h⁡(p),p)H(h(p),p)=0=-pF_{1}(h(p),p)-(1-p)F_{2}(h(p),p). It means that the states p0=0p^{0}=0 (only population 22) and p0=1p^{0}=1 (only population 11) are equilibria for this system.

Moreover,

r′​(0)=F1​(h⁡(0),0)r^{\prime}(0)=F_{1}(h(0),0)

and

r′​(1)=h′​(1)​∂nF1​(h⁡(1),1)+∂pF1​(h⁡(1),1).r^{\prime}(1)=h^{\prime}(1)\partial_{n}F_{1}(h(1),1)+\partial_{p}F_{1}(h(1),1).

Hence under some direct sign assumptions on F1F_{1} and ∂pF1\partial_{p}F_{1}, the equilibria 00 and 11 for pp can be made stable in the limit equation, if r′​(0)r^{\prime}(0) and r′​(1)r^{\prime}(1) are negative. In particular, in the example in Section 3, the function rr is bistable.

Remark 2.

The assumption ninit,ϵ−h⁡(0)n^{\text{init},\epsilon}-h(0) uniformly bounded with respect to ϵ\epsilon in L2​(ℝd)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) together with the uniform bound of pinit,ϵp^{\text{init},\epsilon} in L2​(ℝd)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) imply, thanks to Assumption 3, that ninit−h⁡(pinit,ϵ)n^{\text{init}}-h(p^{\text{init},\epsilon}) is bounded in L2​(ℝd)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), uniformly in ϵ>0\epsilon>0. Remark 3.

One might be interested by the effect of the local introduction of a variant into a population at equilibrium. In this situation, at the time of introduction, variant 22 is at equilibrium whereas the introduction of variant 11 is modeled by a compactly supported continuous nonnegative function ϕ\phi. Then we have n2init,ϵ=1ϵ−h⁡(0)n_{2}^{\text{init},\epsilon}=\frac{1}{\epsilon}-h(0) on ℝd∖supp ​ϕ\mathbb{R}^{d}\setminus\mbox{supp }\phi, and we set n1init,ϵ=ϕ​n2init,ϵn_{1}^{\text{init},\epsilon}=\phi n_{2}^{\text{init},\epsilon}. Then, pinit=ϕ1+ϕp^{\text{init}}=\frac{\phi}{1+\phi} and assumption (11) in Theorem 1 boils down to assuming that

1ϵ−(1+ϕ)​n2init,ϵ−h⁡(0)​ is uniformly bounded with respect to ​ϵ​ in ​L∞​(ℝd).\frac{1}{\epsilon}-(1+\phi)n_{2}^{\text{init},\epsilon}-h(0)\mbox{ is uniformly bounded with respect to }\epsilon\mbox{ in }L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).

Finally, we mention that we can relax the assumption (11) by assuming that the sequence (pinit,ϵ)ϵ(p^{\text{init},\epsilon})_{\epsilon} is uniformly bounded with respect to ϵ\epsilon in L2​(ℝd)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) instead of assuming its convergence. In fact, we can extract a subsequence of (pinit,ϵ)ϵ(p^{\text{init},\epsilon})_{\epsilon} that converges weakly towards pinitp^{\text{init}} and the result applies. But the uniqueness of the weak limit pinitp^{\text{init}} is not guaranteed and therefore, the result in Theorem 1 is available only up to an extraction of a subsequence.

3 Application to a biological example

3.1 Presentation of the model

We consider the case of Wolbachia in arthropod species (for the biology of this bacterium, see [23] ; for mathematical modeling, see [2], [5], [13], [3]). It is an endo-symbiont that is maternally transmitted, causes cytoplasmic incompatibility (CI), and has several other effects on its host. Here, we understand CI as a mechanism through which one of the possible crossings is less viable. More precisely, if an uninfected female is fertilized by an infected male, a fraction only of its eggs will eventually hatch and give birth to viable larvae. For more details about CI, we refer to [23]. In the case of Aedes mosquitoes, Wolbachia reduces lifespan, changes fecundity and blocks the development of dengue virus (see [16], [22], [14]). It is then a potential biological tool to fight dengue epidemics. However, it does not change the way mosquitoes move. Therefore, in order to model a Wolbachia invasion (assessed in the field in [12]) we are precisely in our setting. Several (two) variants of the same species interact with each other in a complex way.

Specifically, we define the uninfected death rate dud_{u}. This rate is multiplied by δ>1\delta>1 for infected mosquitoes: di=δ​dud_{i}=\delta d_{u}. We also define an uninfected fecundity FuF_{u} for uninfected mosquitoes, Fi=(1−sf)​FuF_{i}=(1-s_{f})F_{u} for infected mosquitoes ; a resource parameter σ\sigma ; and a CI parameter 0<sh≤10<s_{h}\leq 1, which means that a fraction shs_{h} of uninfected females’ eggs fertilized by infected males won’t hatch. Parameters δ\delta, sfs_{f} and shs_{h} have been estimated in several cases and can be found in the literature (see [2] and references therein). We will always assume sh>sfs_{h}>s_{f}. (In practice, we usually have sfs_{f} close to 00 and shs_{h} close to 11). Let us denote ni​(t,x)n_{i}(t,x), resp. nu​(t,x)n_{u}(t,x), the density of the infected, resp. uninfected, mosquitoes at time t≥0t\geq 0, position x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

Several models have been written, using these parameters. In [3] (if we ignore the drift speed v∈ℝdv\in\mathbb{R}^{d} they used, which amounts at a change of coordinates) one find

{∂tni−∇⋅(A(x)∇ni)=ni(1−σ(nu+ni))−duni,∂tnu−∇⋅(A(x)∇nu)=nuFu(1−shninu+ni)(1−σ(nu+ni))−dunu.\begin{cases}&\partial_{t}n_{i}-\nabla\cdot(A(x)\nabla n_{i})=n_{i}(1-\sigma(n_{u}+n_{i}))-d_{u}n_{i},\\ &\partial_{t}n_{u}-\nabla\cdot(A(x)\nabla n_{u})=n_{u}F_{u}(1-s_{h}\frac{n_{i}}{n_{u}+n_{i}})(1-\sigma(n_{u}+n_{i}))-d_{u}n_{u}.\end{cases} (14)

In this model, δ=1\delta=1 and variables are scaled so that Fu​(1−sf)=Fi=1F_{u}(1-s_{f})=F_{i}=1. Here the reduced population is defined by n=1σ−(ni+nu)n=\frac{1}{\sigma}-(n_{i}+n_{u}). The corresponding dynamics in (n,p)(n,p) for (14) is written

{∂tn−∇⋅(A(x)∇n)=(σn(p+Fu(1−p)(1−shp))−du),∂tp−∇⋅(A(x)∇p)+2∇nnA(x)∇p=σnp(1−p)(du−Fu(1−shp)),\begin{cases}&\partial_{t}n-\nabla\cdot(A(x)\nabla n)=\big(\sigma n(p+F_{u}(1-p)(1-s_{h}p))-d_{u}\big),\\ &\partial_{t}p-\nabla\cdot(A(x)\nabla p)+2\frac{\nabla n}{n}A(x)\nabla p=\sigma np(1-p)\big(d_{u}-F_{u}(1-s_{h}p)\big),\end{cases} (15)

In (15), the reaction term for pp depends on nn merely for its intensity (it is a multiplicative factor). In particular, the unstable steady state (defining, in some sense, a possible “threshold for invasion”) is equal to 1sh​(1−duFu)\frac{1}{s_{h}}(1-\frac{d_{u}}{F_{u}}) does not depend on nn.

To further reduce this class of models and prove the convergence towards (3), we introduce the parameter ϵ\epsilon to characterize the high fertility and competition that result in a carrying capacity of order 1ϵ\frac{1}{\epsilon}. Then we propose the following generalization of (14), which incorporates also the different death rate and the reduction of fecundity,

{∂tni−∇⋅(A(x)∇ni)=(1−sf)​Fu​ni​(1ϵ−σ⁡(ni+nu))−δ​du​ni,∂tnu−∇⋅(A(x)∇nu)=Fu​nu​(1−sh​nini+nu)​(1ϵ−σ⁡(ni+nu))−du​nu,\begin{cases}\partial_{t}n_{i}-\nabla\cdot(A(x)\nabla n_{i})&=(1-s_{f})F_{u}n_{i}\big(\frac{1}{\epsilon}-\sigma(n_{i}+n_{u})\big)-\delta d_{u}n_{i},\\ \partial_{t}n_{u}-\nabla\cdot(A(x)\nabla n_{u})&=F_{u}n_{u}(1-s_{h}\frac{n_{i}}{n_{i}+n_{u}})\big(\frac{1}{\epsilon}-\sigma(n_{i}+n_{u})\big)-d_{u}n_{u},\\ \end{cases} (16)

Straightforwardly, we can compute the equilibria for the associated dynamical system.

Lemma 2.

As soon as sf+δ−1<δ​shs_{f}+\delta-1<\delta s_{h}, there are four distinct equilibria associated with (16) in the non-negative quadrant.

  • •

    Wolbachia invasion steady state (ni​W∗,nu​W∗):=(1σ​ϵ−duFu​δ1−sf,0)(n^{*}_{iW},n^{*}_{uW}):=(\frac{1}{\sigma\epsilon}-\frac{d_{u}}{F_{u}}\frac{\delta}{1-s_{f}},0) is stable;

  • •

    Wolbachia extinction steady state (ni​E∗,nu​E∗):=(0,1σ​ϵ−duFu)(n^{*}_{iE},n^{*}_{uE}):=(0,\frac{1}{\sigma\epsilon}-\frac{d_{u}}{F_{u}}) is stable;

  • •

    The co-existence steady state (ni​C∗,nu​C∗):=((1σ​ϵ−duFu​δ1−sf)​δ−(1−sf)δ​sh,(1σ​ϵ−duFu​δ1−sf)​δ⁡(sh−1)+(1−sf)δ​sh)(n^{*}_{iC},n^{*}_{uC}):=\big(\big(\frac{1}{\sigma\epsilon}-\frac{d_{u}}{F_{u}}\frac{\delta}{1-s_{f}}\big)\frac{\delta-(1-s_{f})}{\delta s_{h}},\big(\frac{1}{\sigma\epsilon}-\frac{d_{u}}{F_{u}}\frac{\delta}{1-s_{f}}\big)\frac{\delta(s_{h}-1)+(1-s_{f})}{\delta s_{h}}\big) is unstable;

  • •

    The steady state (0,0)(0,0) is unstable.

3.2 Large population asymptotic

We perform the limit ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0 for system (16). To recover notations from Theorem 1, we identify n1=nin_{1}=n_{i}, n2=nun_{2}=n_{u}. As above we define the reduced quantity n=1σ​ϵ−(n1+n2)n=\frac{1}{\sigma\epsilon}-(n_{1}+n_{2}) and p=n1n1+n2p=\frac{n_{1}}{n_{1}+n_{2}}. Then with the notations in Section 2, one has

F1​(n,p)\displaystyle F_{1}(n,p) =σ​n​(1−sf)​Fu−δ​du,\displaystyle=\sigma n(1-s_{f})F_{u}-\delta d_{u},
F2​(n,p)\displaystyle F_{2}(n,p) =σ​n​Fu​(1−sh​p)−du.\displaystyle=\sigma nF_{u}(1-s_{h}p)-d_{u}.

Therefore, by definition (8), we compute

H⁡(n,p)\displaystyle H(n,p) =−p⁡(σ​n​(1−sf)​Fu−δ​du)−(1−p)​(σ​n​Fu​(1−sh​p)−du)\displaystyle=-p(\sigma n(1-s_{f})F_{u}-\delta d_{u})-(1-p)(\sigma nF_{u}(1-s_{h}p)-d_{u})
=−σ​Fu​n​(sh​p2−(sf+sh)​p+1)+du​((δ−1)​p+1).\displaystyle=-\sigma F_{u}n(s_{h}p^{2}-(s_{f}+s_{h})p+1)+d_{u}((\delta-1)p+1).

And Assumption 6 is satisfied. Then, Assumption 3 is easy to check since H⁡(0,p)=du​((δ−1)​p+1)>0H(0,p)=d_{u}((\delta-1)p+1)>0 and using the fact that the polynomial x↦sh​x2−(sf+sh)​x+1x\mapsto s_{h}x^{2}-(s_{f}+s_{h})x+1 is minimal for x=sf+sh2​shx=\frac{s_{f}+s_{h}}{2s_{h}}, we have

∂nH⁡(n,p)=−σ​Fu​(sh​p2−(sf+sh)​p+1)≤−σ​Fu​(1−(sf+sh)24​sh)<0,\partial_{n}H(n,p)=-\sigma F_{u}(s_{h}p^{2}-(s_{f}+s_{h})p+1)\leq-\sigma F_{u}(1-\frac{(s_{f}+s_{h})^{2}}{4s_{h}})<0,

since we have sf<shs_{f}<s_{h}. We notice also that this computation implies that the above second order polynomial in pp is always away from 00 on [0,1][0,1]. Moreover, recalling the definition H⁡(n,p)=0H(n,p)=0 if and only if n=h⁡(p)n=h(p) from Assumption 3, we can compute h⁡(p)=duσ​Fu​(δ−1)​p+1sh​p2−(sf+sh)​p+1.h(p)=\frac{d_{u}}{\sigma F_{u}}\frac{(\delta-1)p+1}{s_{h}p^{2}-(s_{f}+s_{h})p+1}. Under Assumption 1 on AA, Theorem 1 applies, and pϵp^{\epsilon} converges towards the solution of the following equation

{∂tp0−∇⋅(A(x)∇p0)=r⁡(p0),p0​(t=0)=pinit,\left\{\begin{array}[]{rcl}\partial_{t}p^{0}-\nabla\cdot(A(x)\nabla p^{0})&=&r(p^{0}),\\ p^{0}(t=0)&=&p^{\text{init}},\end{array}\right. (17)

and the reaction term writes

r⁡(p)=δ​du​sh​p​(1−p)​(p−θ)sh​p2−(sf+sh)​p+1,θ=sf+δ−1δ​sh,r(p)=\delta d_{u}s_{h}\frac{p(1-p)(p-\theta)}{s_{h}p^{2}-(s_{f}+s_{h})p+1},\qquad\theta=\frac{s_{f}+\delta-1}{\delta s_{h}},

which is bistable provided δ\delta satisfies the condition from Lemma 2:

sf+δ−1<δ​sh.s_{f}+\delta-1<\delta s_{h}. (18)

If δ=1\delta=1, we find the ubiquitous value θ(=p∗)=sfsh\theta(=p^{*})=\frac{s_{f}}{s_{h}}, which corresponds to the model of spacial spread of Wolbachia proposed in [2]. In addition, this expression is coherent with the one in [19] for general δ\delta. Even though the equation for pp has already been suggested for a while, as far as we know, no convergence result as ours had been proved before from a two-populations model to the bistable equation.

A direct application of Theorem 1 establishes that, in the limit ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0, the derivation in [2] holds true in a strong topology.

Corollary 1.

Assume that AA satisfies Assumption 1. Given n1init,ϵn_{1}^{\text{init},\epsilon} and n2init,ϵn_{2}^{\text{init},\epsilon} such that there exists pinit∈L2​(ℝd)p^{\text{init}}\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) such that pinit,ϵ⇀pinitp^{\text{init},\epsilon}\rightharpoonup p^{\text{init}} as ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0 in L2​(ℝd)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})-weak and 1σ​ϵ−n1init,ϵ−n2init,ϵ−duσ​Fu∈L2∩L∞​(ℝd)\frac{1}{\sigma\epsilon}-n_{1}^{\text{init},\epsilon}-n_{2}^{\text{init},\epsilon}-\frac{d_{u}}{\sigma F_{u}}\in L^{2}\cap L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) with uniform bounds in ϵ>0\epsilon>0, then Theorem 1 applies and the solutions (niϵ,nuϵ)ϵ>0(n_{i}^{\epsilon},n_{u}^{\epsilon})_{\epsilon>0} of (16) satisfy the convergence result in (12) where the limiting equation is given in (17).

3.3 Numerical illustration

A numerical illustration of this convergence result is shown in Figure 1. Parameters are fixed according to biologically relevant data (freely adapted from [8]). Time unit is the day, and parameters per day are Fi=Fu=1.12F_{i}=F_{u}=1.12 (hence sf=0s_{f}=0), du=.27d_{u}=.27 and di=.3d_{i}=.3, then δ=didu=109\delta=\frac{d_{i}}{d_{u}}=\frac{10}{9}. We choose sf=.1s_{f}=.1 and sh=.8s_{h}=.8. We take σ=1\sigma=1, and A⁡(x)≡.1A(x)\equiv.1, which amounts at choosing a space scale.

We discretize the one-dimensional computational domain [−15;15][-15;15] with space step Δ​x=.05\Delta x=.05 and take a time step Δ​t=.005\Delta t=.005. The reaction diffusion equations are discretized thanks to semi-implicit finite difference scheme, the diffusion operator being treated implicitly (to avoid too restrictive stability conditions), while the reaction term is treated explicitly. Curves are plotted every 50005000 iterations, at times (in days) T1=25T_{1}=25, T2=50T_{2}=50, T3=75T_{3}=75, T4=100T_{4}=100 and T5=125T_{5}=125. We display 4 numerical tests with the same initial data pinitp^{\text{init}} compactly supported, plotted in pluses (+). The blue lines represent the solution of the limiting system (17). In dashed red lines are plotted the computed fraction p=nini+nup=\frac{n_{i}}{n_{i}+n_{u}} where (ni,nu)(n_{i},n_{u}) solves the system of two populations (16). In this computation the initial data are taken as noticed in Remark 3: we consider the compactly supported function ϕ=pinit/(1−pinit)\phi=p^{\text{init}}/(1-p^{\text{init}}) and for given nuinitn_{u}^{\text{init}} we take niinit=ϕ​nuinitn_{i}^{\text{init}}=\phi n_{u}^{\text{init}}. We observe that the solution of the limiting bistable system (17) exhibits a traveling front which propagates into the whole domain. Then the numerical results for 4 different values of the parameter ϵ\epsilon are represented. For large populations, we observe that as ϵ\epsilon goes to 00 (recall that the order of magnitude of the population size is 1σ​ϵ\frac{1}{\sigma\epsilon}), the solution to the whole system (16) gets closer to the one of the limiting system. However, for ϵ=.6\epsilon=.6, the introduced population goes extinct, and pp does not behave as in the limiting model. This illustrates how the 2 by 2 system qualitatively differs from the limit reaction-diffusion equation.

An additional conclusion we can draw from Figure 1 is that our approximation result will always be local in time. Indeed, for small ϵ\epsilon we see a traveling wave appear in dashed red, that has a slower speed than the blue one. Hence the norm of their difference will be constantly growing in time.

4 Proof of convergence

This Section is devoted to the proof of Theorem 1. We write the system of equations satisfied by (nϵ,pϵ)(n^{\epsilon},p^{\epsilon})

{∂tnϵ−∇⋅(A(x)∇nϵ)=(1ϵ−nϵ)H(nϵ,pϵ),∂tpϵ−∇⋅(A(x)∇pϵ)+2ϵ∇pϵ⋅A(x)∇nϵ1−ϵ​nϵ=pϵ(1−pϵ)(F1−F2)(nϵ,pϵ),nϵ(t=0)=ninit,ϵ,pϵ(t=0)=pinit,ϵ.\begin{cases}\partial_{t}n^{\epsilon}-\nabla\cdot(A(x)\nabla n^{\epsilon})=\big(\frac{1}{\epsilon}-n^{\epsilon}\big)H(n^{\epsilon},p^{\epsilon}),\\[5.69054pt] \partial_{t}p^{\epsilon}-\nabla\cdot(A(x)\nabla p^{\epsilon})+2\epsilon\nabla p^{\epsilon}\cdot\frac{A(x)\nabla n^{\epsilon}}{1-\epsilon n^{\epsilon}}=p^{\epsilon}(1-p^{\epsilon})\big(F_{1}-F_{2}\big)(n^{\epsilon},p^{\epsilon}),\\[5.69054pt] n^{\epsilon}(t=0)=n^{\text{init},\epsilon},\qquad p^{\epsilon}(t=0)=p^{\text{init},\epsilon}\,.\end{cases} (19)

We recall that the initial data are assumed to satisfy (11). Then the sequence (pinit,ϵ)ϵ(p^{\text{init},\epsilon})_{\epsilon} is bounded uniformly in ϵ\epsilon in L2​(ℝd)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and (ninit,ϵ−h⁡(0))ϵ(n^{\text{init},\epsilon}-h(0))_{\epsilon} is bounded uniformly in ϵ\epsilon in L2∩L∞​(ℝd)L^{2}\cap L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). The proof of Theorem 1 relies strongly on a sequence of a priori estimates uniform in ϵ\epsilon, which give compactness and allow to pass to the limit in the equation for pϵp^{\epsilon}.

From now on, we will drop the superscript ϵ\epsilon in the notations.

4.1 Estimates

For ϵ>0\epsilon>0 fixed, existence of solutions to (19) is classical (see e.g. [18]). Now we establish some a priori estimates uniform in ϵ>0\epsilon>0. First, we have the following L∞L^{\infty} bounds.

∀t>0,x∈ℝd, 0≤p⁡(t,x)≤1\forall t>0,x\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\,0\leq p(t,x)\leq 1

Then y⁡(0)=0y(0)=0. We deduce that y≡0y\equiv 0.

Before proving our main result, we recall the following compactness result (see [20]).

We split the proof into three steps. First, our previous estimates together with Lions-Aubin lemma enable us to prove relative compactness on bounded domains. Finally, thanks to our uniform estimates, we prove that this limit satisfies a universal equation whose solution is unique, which in turn implies convergence of the whole sequence.

5 Generalization of the result

We have stated Theorem 1 so as to keep simplicity and stick to the biological application in Section 3. It can be slightly generalized in order to encompass spontaneous transition between variants.

Individuals in state 11 may give birth to individuals in state 22, and vice versa. To do so, we consider more general reaction term and replace system (1) by

{∂tn1−∇⋅(A(x)∇n1)=f~1​(n1,n2),∂tn2−∇⋅(A(x)∇n2)=f~2​(n1,n2),\begin{cases}\partial_{t}n_{1}-\nabla\cdot(A(x)\nabla n_{1})&=\widetilde{f}_{1}(n_{1},n_{2}),\\ \partial_{t}n_{2}-\nabla\cdot(A(x)\nabla n_{2})&=\widetilde{f}_{2}(n_{1},n_{2}),\end{cases}

In fact, the basic property we require in our proof is that pp stays between 00 and 11, that is, nin_{i} remain non-negative. Here is the minimal hypothesis ensuring positivity (in the spirit of [18]).

Assumption 4 (Positivity).

We assume

∀n1,n2∈ℝ+,f~1​(0,n2)≥0​ and ​f~2​(n1,0)≥0.\forall n_{1},n_{2}\in\mathbb{R}_{+},\quad\widetilde{f}_{1}(0,n_{2})\geq 0\mbox{ and }\widetilde{f}_{2}(n_{1},0)\geq 0.
Proof of “Assumption 4 implies positivity“.

We prove that if the initial data n1initn_{1}^{\text{init}}, n2initn_{2}^{\text{init}} are non-negative and if Assumption 4 holds, then n1n_{1} and n2n_{2} remain non-negative. It is a simple application of the comparison principle for this parabolic system. A solution that lies initially above a sub-solution remains above it. The constant (0,0)(0,0) is indeed a sub-solution. ∎

For the sake of clarity of the presentation, we only consider an extension of the biological example from Section 3. This allows us to take into account imperfect maternal transmission. We assume that at a rate μ\mu, infected females lay eggs which do not carry Wolbachia. This quantity is very commonly tested by entomologists, and usually shown to be close to 00 (see [23] and references, and for example [4] where they obtained μ=0.04\mu=0.04 and μ=0\mu=0). This feature is included in the following model taken from [5] (neglecting the pathogen effect),

{∂tni−∇⋅(A(x)∇ni)=niFu(1−sf)(1−μ)−ni(di+σ(ni+nu)),∂tnu−∇⋅(A(x)∇nu)=nuFu(1−shninu+ni)+μFu(1−sf)ni−nu(du+σ(ni+nu)).\begin{cases}&\partial_{t}n_{i}-\nabla\cdot(A(x)\nabla n_{i})=n_{i}F_{u}(1-s_{f})(1-\mu)-n_{i}(d_{i}+\sigma(n_{i}+n_{u})),\\ &\partial_{t}n_{u}-\nabla\cdot(A(x)\nabla n_{u})=n_{u}F_{u}(1-s_{h}\frac{n_{i}}{n_{u}+n_{i}})+\mu F_{u}(1-s_{f})n_{i}-n_{u}(d_{u}+\sigma(n_{i}+n_{u})).\end{cases} (33)

Here, the reduced population would be n=σ⁡(ni+nu)n=\sigma(n_{i}+n_{u}). The corresponding dynamics in (n,p)(n,p) reads,

{∂tn−∇⋅(A(x)∇n)=n(Fu(p(1−sf)+(1−p)(1−shp))−du((δ−1)p+1)−n),∂tp−∇⋅(A(x)∇p)−2∇nnA(x)∇p=p((1−p)(Fu(1−shp)−du(δ−1))−μFu(1−sf)).\begin{cases}&\partial_{t}n-\nabla\cdot(A(x)\nabla n)=n\Big(F_{u}\big(p(1-s_{f})+(1-p)(1-s_{h}p)\big)-d_{u}\big((\delta-1)p+1\big)-n\Big),\\ &\partial_{t}p-\nabla\cdot(A(x)\nabla p)-2\frac{\nabla n}{n}A(x)\nabla p=p\Big((1-p)\big(F_{u}(1-s_{h}p)-d_{u}(\delta-1)\big)-\mu F_{u}(1-s_{f})\Big).\end{cases} (34)

We give a numerical illustration of this case in Figure 2, using a similar approach as in Section 3.3. We use the same parameters as for Figure 1, except that sf=0s_{f}=0, μ=.04\mu=.04 and the initial data is smaller (less infected mosquitoes are introduced).

For Figure 2, we use the same discretization and numerical scheme as in Figure 1. The blue lines represent the solution of the limiting system (38). In dashed red lines are plotted the numerical results for the system of two populations (37). We observe that the solution of the limiting bistable system (38) exhibits a traveling front which propagates into the whole domain. Then the numerical results for 4 different values of the parameter ϵ\epsilon are represented. For large populations, we observe that as ϵ\epsilon goes to 00 (recall that the order of magnitude of the population size is 1σ​ϵ\frac{1}{\sigma\epsilon}), the solution to the whole system (37) gets closer to the one of the limiting system. However, for small populations, we see a clear modification of the wave’s shape and speed, which is slower than the limit wave.

6 Conclusion and perspectives

We have established in this paper the rigorous convergence, under suitable assumptions, of a 2 by 2 reaction diffusion model of Lotka-Volterra type towards a simple model for the frequency of a variant. It justifies the use of such reduced model in applications. Let us discuss quickly our scaling choice in Assumption 6, in the case of Wolbachia.

Another biologically relevant scaling assumption would not give a limiting system consisting in only one equation on frequency. Indeed, if we consider the following alternative model

{∂tni−∇⋅(A(x)∇ni)=(1−sf)​Fu​ni​(1−ϵ​σ​(ni+nu))−δ​du​ni,∂tnu−∇⋅(A(x)∇nu)=Fu​nu​(1−sh​nini+nu)​(1−ϵ​σ​(ni+nu))−du​nu.\begin{cases}\partial_{t}n_{i}-\nabla\cdot(A(x)\nabla n_{i})&=(1-s_{f})F_{u}n_{i}\big(1-\epsilon\sigma(n_{i}+n_{u})\big)-\delta d_{u}n_{i},\\ \partial_{t}n_{u}-\nabla\cdot(A(x)\nabla n_{u})&=F_{u}n_{u}(1-s_{h}\frac{n_{i}}{n_{i}+n_{u}})\big(1-\epsilon\sigma(n_{i}+n_{u})\big)-d_{u}n_{u}.\\ \end{cases} (39)

Then, nn and pp satisfy the following system, that does not depend on ϵ\epsilon

{∂tn−∇⋅(A(x)∇n)=Fu(1−n)(A(p)−B(p)n),∂tp−∇⋅(A(x)∇p)+2∇p⋅A(x)∇n1−n=p(1−p)(Fun(shp−sf)−du(δ−1)),\begin{cases}\partial_{t}n-\nabla\cdot(A(x)\nabla n)=F_{u}\big(1-n\big)\big(A(p)-B(p)n\big),\\ \partial_{t}p-\nabla\cdot(A(x)\nabla p)+\frac{2\nabla p\cdot A(x)\nabla n}{1-n}=p(1-p)\big(F_{u}n(s_{h}p-s_{f})-d_{u}(\delta-1)\big),\\ \end{cases} (40)

where

{A⁡(p)=((δ−1)​p+1)​duFu,B⁡(p)=sh​p2−(sf+sh)​p+1.\begin{cases}A(p)&=((\delta-1)p+1)\frac{d_{u}}{F_{u}},\\ B(p)&=s_{h}p^{2}-(s_{f}+s_{h})p+1.\\ \end{cases}

The dependancy in ϵ\epsilon in the resulting model is only through the initial data. Thus, ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0 does not imply n−A⁡(p)B⁡(p)→0n-\frac{A(p)}{B(p)}\to 0 in (39), (40).

We conclude that the use of simple bistable models for the spatial spread of Wolbachia can be justified mathematically. This is the object of Theorem 1. However, we must keep in mind that this result applies only if population size and fecundity scale properly.

In the context of Wolbachia modeling, bistable equations like (3) have been used (for example in [2] or [19]) because they provide with a unique (up to translations) and linearly stable traveling wave solution. Hence, with a bistable model at hand we can compute a speed that may be interpreted as an invasion speed.

Therefore a natural continuation of the present work would be to try and specify Theorem 1 to traveling waves. The open question reads: does the frequency in the two-populations model converge to the unique traveling wave solution of the limit bistable equation? If yes, in what sense? Indeed, there are two types of convergence involved: on the first hand in the singular limit (where we identified a small parameter ϵ\epsilon), that proves convergence of the system’s frequency to a solution of the limit bistable equation; and on the other hand the well-known attractiveness result of the unique traveling wave solution in the bistable case. Moreover, existence and (local) stability of traveling waves has been proved for competitive systems (see [9] for example). How to compare the traveling speed for competitive system with the one for the reduced model on the frequency?
